findings.title: Chore completions are never modelled; the UI fabricates completion counts from cents
findings.body_md: The elementary fact "child completed chore X at time T" is never recorded anywhere: completing a chore only increments `Child.totalCents`. Because the fact is missing, `HomePage.tsx:78` and `TotalsPage.tsx:77` invent a count with `Math.floor(child.totalCents / 100)` (commented "Rough estimate") and display it as "N done" / "N chores completed". Any chore not valued at exactly 100 cents makes the displayed count wrong. Model a Completion record (childId, choreId, valueCents, createdAt) or stop displaying a count the data cannot support.
findings.issue_title: Chore completions are not stored, so displayed completion counts are fabricated
findings.issue_body: The data model records only an aggregate `Child.totalCents`; individual chore completions are never persisted. `client/src/pages/HomePage.tsx:78` and `client/src/pages/TotalsPage.tsx:77` therefore estimate "chores completed" as `Math.floor(totalCents / 100)`, which is wrong for any chore not worth exactly $1 (the seeded list includes $5 chores). Users see completion counts that do not match reality, and no history view of completions is possible. Either add a completions store (childId, choreId, valueCents, createdAt) and derive counts from it, or remove the fabricated "N done" / "N chores completed" figures from the UI.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes a data model under design; the model lives at `shared/schema.ts` and is persisted via `client/src/lib/db.ts`.

findings.title: No uniqueness beyond surrogate ids; duplicate children and chores are freely representable
findings.body_md: Every store's only key is a generated nanoid; nothing asserts what makes a row one thing. Two children with the same name, or two chores with the same title and value, are freely representable and indistinguishable in the UI (cards show initials and name only). A duplicate submission creates a second identical child with its own balance. Add an application-level uniqueness check on child name (and optionally chore title) at creation time, since IndexedDB cannot express the constraint declaratively on a non-key field without an index.
findings.issue_title: Nothing prevents duplicate child names or duplicate chores
findings.issue_body: All IndexedDB stores (`client/src/lib/db.ts:40-57`) are keyed only by a generated nanoid, and no write path checks natural uniqueness. Adding a child with an existing name silently creates a second, indistinguishable child with its own separate balance, which reads as a data bug to the user. Add a case-insensitive duplicate-name check in `AppStorage.createChild` (and consider the same for chore titles), surfacing a clear error in `AddChildDialog`.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes fact types with keys; the IndexedDB stores at `client/src/lib/db.ts:40-57` are keyed only by generated `id`.

findings.title: Zod value constraints exist but guard no write path; import writes unvalidated JSON
findings.body_md: The bounds written in `shared/schema.ts` (non-negative integer cents, minimum chore value) are never enforced at a write path: `AddChildDialog` and `AddChoreDialog` do their own ad hoc checks, and the import path (`SettingsPage.tsx:117-120`) does `JSON.parse` then `importData(data)` with no `appDataSchema.parse` at all, so any malformed or hostile backup file is written straight into IndexedDB. A backup with `totalCents: -500`, string cents, or missing fields corrupts the store and breaks pages that assume the schema. Parse imports with `appDataSchema` before writing, and route dialog validation through the insert schemas.
findings.issue_title: Backup import bypasses schema validation and can write malformed data
findings.issue_body: `client/src/pages/SettingsPage.tsx:117-120` reads the chosen backup file, calls `JSON.parse`, and hands the result directly to `AppStorage.importData`, which writes it into IndexedDB without validating against `appDataSchema` (`shared/schema.ts:65-71`). The Zod bounds on `totalCents` and `valueCents` therefore guard nothing: a malformed or edited backup can set negative balances, non-integer cents, or drop required fields, corrupting the store and crashing pages that assume the shape. Validate with `appDataSchema.safeParse` before importing and reject the file with a clear error when it fails.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes domain-bounded values; `shared/schema.ts:7` bounds `totalCents` at `int().min(0)` and `shared/schema.ts:26` bounds `valueCents` at `min(1)`.

findings.title: Payout rows duplicate the child's name with no invalidation story
findings.body_md: `Payout.childName` depends on `childId`, not on the payout key: a classic transitive dependency stored without a recorded decision. Today there is no rename path so it cannot drift, but the schema permits drift the moment one is added, and the duplication serves no purpose because deleting a child also deletes their payouts (`client/src/lib/storage.ts:57-67`), so the snapshot never outlives the child it snapshots. Either drop `childName` and join on `childId` at display time, or record the snapshot as a deliberate denormalisation and keep payouts when a child is deleted so the snapshot has a reason to exist.
findings.issue_title: Payout.childName duplicates child data and the duplication serves no purpose
findings.issue_body: `shared/schema.ts:42` stores `childName` on every payout alongside `childId`. Duplicating the name only makes sense as a snapshot that survives the child, but `AppStorage.deleteChild` (`client/src/lib/storage.ts:57-67`) deletes all of a child's payouts with them, so the snapshot never outlives its source; meanwhile any future rename feature will silently desynchronise history from the child list. Either resolve the name via `childId` at display time, or keep payout history on child deletion so the snapshot is doing real work, and note the choice in the schema.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes non-key attributes mapped to storage; `payoutSchema` at `shared/schema.ts:39-45` stores both `childId` and `childName`.

findings.title: Deleting a chore leaves dangling ids in every child's favourites list
findings.body_md: `AppStorage.deleteChore` deletes the chore row but never removes its id from any child's `favoriteChoreIds`, so favourites accumulate references to chores that no longer exist. Display code tolerates it (favourites are computed by filtering live chores), but the dangling ids grow without bound and any future consumer that trusts the list gets phantom favourites. When deleting a chore, sweep all children and strip the id from `favoriteChoreIds` in the same operation.
findings.issue_title: deleteChore does not clean up favoriteChoreIds references
findings.issue_body: `client/src/lib/storage.ts:118-121` deletes a chore without removing its id from children's `favoriteChoreIds` arrays, unlike `deleteChild`, which does clean up its dependent payouts. The dangling ids are currently masked because favourites are computed by filtering live chores, but they accumulate indefinitely and will surface as phantom favourites in any code that reads the list directly. In `deleteChore`, load all children and strip the deleted id from each `favoriteChoreIds` before completing.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes relationships wired in code; `Child.favoriteChoreIds` (`shared/schema.ts:8`) references chore ids, and chores are deletable at `client/src/lib/storage.ts:118-121`.

findings.title: Multi-step writes are not transactional; a failed import destroys all existing data
findings.body_md: `importData` clears `children`, `chores` and `payouts` in separate auto-committed transactions, then re-adds rows in yet more transactions: any failure after the clears (malformed row, quota error, tab close) leaves the user with their old data destroyed and the import partial, with no rollback. `payoutChild` creates the payout record and zeroes the balance as two separate transactions, so an interruption between them records a payout while leaving the balance intact, inviting a double payout. `completeChore` is an unguarded read-modify-write on `totalCents`. IndexedDB supports a single `readwrite` transaction spanning multiple stores; wrap each of these operations in one.
findings.issue_title: importData and payoutChild are not atomic; mid-operation failure corrupts or destroys data
findings.issue_body: In `client/src/lib/storage.ts`, `importData` (:202-232) clears three IndexedDB stores and repopulates them across many separate auto-committed transactions, so a failure after the clears (bad row, quota, tab close) permanently destroys the user's existing data with the import only partially applied. `payoutChild` (:246-265) creates the payout row and zeroes `totalCents` in two separate transactions, so an interruption can record a payout without resetting the balance, and `completeChore` (:235-244) is an unguarded read-modify-write. IndexedDB allows one `readwrite` transaction over multiple stores: perform each of these operations inside a single transaction so they commit or roll back as one.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes writes touching more than one store; `importData` (`client/src/lib/storage.ts:202-232`) clears and repopulates three stores, and `payoutChild` (`:246-265`) writes payouts then children.

self_assessment.limits: Verdicts are from static reading; IndexedDB runtime behaviour (transaction interleaving, upgrade paths) was not exercised in a browser.

findings.title: Two real user tiers (parent and child) are collapsed into one all-powerful user
findings.body_md: The app has exactly one capability level: whoever holds the device can complete chores, edit chore values, delete children, and pay out. The child-facing chore page (`ChildChoresPage.tsx:297-322`) exposes the payout flow and chore editing alongside the Complete button a child is meant to tap, so a child can raise their own chore values or pay themselves out. "The user" was never tiered into parent and child, and every requirement inherited the parent's capability. Decide which actions are parent-only (payout, delete, value edits) and gate them, even with something as light as a parent PIN.
findings.issue_title: No parent/child capability split: children can edit values and trigger payouts
findings.issue_body: The app treats every operator identically. On the child's own chore page (`client/src/pages/ChildChoresPage.tsx:297-322`) the payout card, chore editing and chore deletion sit next to the Complete button a child uses, and Settings allows deleting children entirely. In a family chore tracker the natural tiers are parent (manage children, values, payouts) and child (complete chores), and collapsing them means a child with the device can inflate values or pay themselves out. Gate destructive and money-adjacent actions behind a lightweight parent check such as a PIN, and keep the child view to completing chores.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes multiple user tiers; the product is a family chore tracker (client/index.html:7) whose flows are operated both by parents (payouts, settings) and by children (completing chores on their own page).

findings.title: No privacy requirement exists, and bug reports publish user screenshots to a public repository
findings.body_md: Privacy was never specified anywhere, and the consequence is concrete: the in-app bug report captures a full-page screenshot (which shows children's names and balances), then `server/routes/issues.ts:150-166` commits it to the `bug-report-screenshots` branch of the public `rodlunt/choresandrewardsV2` repository and links the raw URL into a public GitHub issue, along with the reporter's user agent, screen resolution and current URL. The form never tells the user any of this will be public. Make the screenshot store private (private repo or object store), state in the form what will be published, and strip or generalise the technical metadata.
findings.issue_title: Bug-report screenshots containing family data are published to a public GitHub repo
findings.issue_body: The bug-report dialog captures a screenshot of the whole page, which for this app typically shows children's names and balances. `server/routes/issues.ts:150-166` then uploads that image to the public `rodlunt/choresandrewardsV2` repository on the `bug-report-screenshots` branch and posts the raw githubusercontent URL into a public issue, together with the reporter's user agent, resolution and page URL (`:92-99`). Nothing in the form (`client/src/components/BugReport.tsx`) warns that the report and image become public. Move screenshots to private storage, add a clear public-disclosure notice to the form, and reduce the technical metadata to what is actually needed.

findings.title: Express error handler responds and then rethrows the same error
findings.body_md: The final error middleware sends the JSON response and then executes `throw err`. The response has already gone out, so the rethrow can only produce noise: Express forwards it to its default handler, which finds headers already sent and dumps a stack, and nothing upstream can recover. Either handle the error (respond and log) or rethrow, not both; here, replace the `throw` with structured logging.
findings.issue_title: Error middleware throws after sending the response
findings.issue_body: `server/index.ts:42-48` responds with the error status and message, then does `throw err` inside the error-handling middleware. Since the response is already sent, the rethrow only reaches Express's default handler, which logs a headers-already-sent style stack trace and adds noise to production logs; no caller can act on it. Remove the `throw` and log the error explicitly instead (with the request path and status), keeping one clear handling path.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes layered error handling; the Express error middleware at `server/index.ts:42-48` is that layer.

findings.title: No required status checks or reviews are enforced on main
findings.body_md: The branch protection on `main` enforces nothing: no required status checks and no required reviews (verified via the GitHub API; only the force-push default applies). With deploys triggered by push to main, a red validate run does not block anything, which is how six weeks of failing gates accumulated without forcing a fix. Require the "Run Pre-Deployment Checks" job as a status check on main so unmergeable red states become visible friction.

findings.issue_body: Branch protection on `main` currently enforces no required status checks and no required reviews (GitHub API confirms only defaults). Since deployment triggers on push to main, nothing forces the failing "Run Pre-Deployment Checks" job to be dealt with, and it has been red since July without blocking merges. Add a branch protection rule (or ruleset) on `main` requiring that job to pass before merge, so a red gate stops the merge instead of failing silently afterwards.

findings.title: A second deploy workflow bypasses the validation gate on every push to main
findings.body_md: Two workflows fire on every push to main: `validate-and-deploy.yml`, whose deploy job correctly declares `needs: validate`, and `deploy.yml`, a standalone "Deploy to Production" workflow with no validation, no audit, and no dependency on anything. The gate the project relies on ("do not bypass the audit") is therefore already bypassed structurally: today `deploy.yml` only fails because the server is unreachable, but the moment issue #29's self-hosted runner lands, it will ship unvalidated code in parallel with (and racing) the gated pipeline, both running `docker-compose down`/`up` on the same host. Delete `deploy.yml` (its job is a strict subset of the gated workflow) before fixing server reachability.
findings.issue_title: deploy.yml deploys without any validation gate and duplicates the gated pipeline
findings.issue_body: `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` triggers on every push to main and SSHes straight into a production `docker-compose down && up --build`, with no type check, no build verification and no security audit. The gated pipeline (`validate-and-deploy.yml`) runs the same deploy behind `needs: validate`, so this second workflow is a structural bypass of the audit gate: it currently fails only because the server is unreachable from GitHub-hosted runners, and once a self-hosted runner is added (issue #29) it would deploy unvalidated code while racing the gated deploy on the same docker-compose project. Delete `deploy.yml` and keep the single gated pipeline; if a manual escape hatch is wanted, keep only its `workflow_dispatch` trigger with an explicit confirmation input.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes a pipeline whose jobs are ordered by declared dependencies; validate-and-deploy.yml:83-86 declares `needs: validate` for exactly this purpose.

findings.title: No concurrency groups; overlapping runs can race the production deploy
findings.body_md: Neither workflow declares a `concurrency` group, so two pushes in quick succession run two full pipelines, and (once the server is reachable) two SSH sessions each executing `docker-compose down && up --build` against the same host, in whatever order they land. Add `concurrency: {group: production-deploy, cancel-in-progress: false}` to the deploy job so deploys serialise, and a cancel-in-progress group on the validate job to drop superseded runs.
findings.issue_title: Add concurrency groups so deploys serialise and stale validations cancel
findings.issue_body: Neither `.github/workflows/validate-and-deploy.yml` nor `deploy.yml` declares `concurrency`. Two quick pushes to main produce overlapping runs; when the server is reachable, each runs `docker-compose down && docker-compose up -d --build` over SSH, and the interleaving can leave the older commit running or the compose project half-down. Add a `concurrency` group named for production deployment with `cancel-in-progress: false` on the deploy job (deploys queue, never interleave) and a `cancel-in-progress: true` group on validation (only the newest commit is checked).
findings.precondition: The rule presumes workflows that can be triggered in overlapping succession; both deploy workflows trigger on every push to main.

findings.title: Workflows run with the default GITHUB_TOKEN scope; no permissions block declared
findings.body_md: No workflow declares a `permissions:` key, so jobs run with whatever default token scope the repository carries. These pipelines only need to read the repo contents; a compromised step (for example via a compromised action tag, see the pinning finding) would hold whatever the default grants. Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of each workflow.
findings.issue_title: Declare least-privilege permissions for GITHUB_TOKEN in workflows
findings.issue_body: Neither workflow in `.github/workflows/` declares a `permissions:` block, so the automatic `GITHUB_TOKEN` runs at the repository default scope. The jobs only read code and deploy over SSH with their own secrets, so the token needs nothing beyond `contents: read`. Add `permissions:\n  contents: read` at workflow level in `validate-and-deploy.yml` (and any other retained workflow) so a compromised step cannot use a broader token.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes GitHub Actions workflows using the automatic token; both workflows in .github/workflows/ do.

findings.title: Third-party actions pinned to mutable tags, not commit SHAs
findings.body_md: All actions are referenced by tag (`actions/checkout@v4`, `pnpm/action-setup@v4`, `appleboy/ssh-action@v1.2.0`). Tags are mutable: a compromised action repo can move one onto malicious code that then runs with this repo's secrets, including the SSH private key to the production server. Pin each action to a full commit SHA (with the tag in a comment) in all workflows.
findings.issue_title: Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs instead of tags
findings.issue_body: Workflows reference actions by mutable tag, e.g. `appleboy/ssh-action@v1.2.0` at `.github/workflows/validate-and-deploy.yml:93`, which handles the production SSH private key. If any of these action repositories is compromised, the tag can be moved to malicious code that exfiltrates the deploy credentials. Replace each tag with the corresponding full commit SHA (keeping the version as a trailing comment), and update via PRs when bumping.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes third-party marketplace actions in production-facing workflows; `appleboy/ssh-action@v1.2.0` and others run in the deploy pipeline.

findings.title: Production deploys are not modelled as a GitHub environment
findings.body_md: The deploy job carries no `environment:` declaration, so the production SSH secrets are repository-wide (available to any workflow, including the ungated `deploy.yml`), and there is no recorded deployment history or optional approval gate. Declare `environment: production` on the deploy job and move `SERVER_HOST`, `SSH_PRIVATE_KEY` and friends into that environment's secrets so only the gated job can read them.
findings.issue_title: Model production as a GitHub environment and scope deploy secrets to it
findings.issue_body: The deploy job in `.github/workflows/validate-and-deploy.yml:83-99` has no `environment:` key, so the SSH credentials for the production server are plain repository secrets readable by every workflow, including the unvalidated `deploy.yml`. Create a `production` environment, move `SERVER_HOST`, `SERVER_USERNAME`, `SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`, `SERVER_PORT` and `DEPLOY_PATH` into it, and add `environment: production` to the gated deploy job. This scopes the secrets to the gated path and gives a recorded deployment history for free.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes production deployments driven from workflows; the deploy job at validate-and-deploy.yml:83-99 targets the production server.

self_assessment.limits: Repository secrets and environment configuration beyond what the API exposes were not inspected; the claim that no environments exist is inferred from the workflows never referencing one.

coverage.note: Read all three workflow files, .gitignore, .github/DEPLOYMENT.md, GITHUB_TOKEN_SETUP.md, rollback scripts and package.json, plus live GitHub state (branch protection API, run history for both deploy workflows, open issues).

findings.title: No security thinking is recorded anywhere for an internet-facing write endpoint
findings.body_md: Nothing in the repository (docs, TODO, issues, code comments) shows any security question being asked before shipping `/api/issues/create`, an internet-reachable endpoint that spends a stored GitHub credential on every call. The concrete consequences are separate findings (no access control, over-scoped token, verbose errors, public screenshots); this finding is the upstream cause. Spend thirty minutes threat-modelling this one endpoint (who can call it, how often, with what payloads, what the token can do) and record the outcome in the repo.
findings.issue_title: Threat-model the /api/issues/create endpoint and record the decisions
findings.issue_body: The only server endpoint, `POST /api/issues/create` (`server/routes/issues.ts:30`), is publicly reachable, unauthenticated, and spends a stored GitHub credential on every call, yet no security consideration for it is recorded anywhere in the repository. Related issues cover the specific defects (access control, token scope, error leakage, screenshot publishing); this one asks for the upstream fix: a short written threat model for the endpoint (callers, abuse cases, rate expectations, blast radius of the token) checked into the repo, with each accepted risk stated.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes security is considered at design time; the repository added a public, unauthenticated POST endpoint that writes to GitHub with a stored credential.

findings.title: The API endpoint validates input with hand-rolled truthiness checks instead of the schema layer the repo already has
findings.body_md: `/api/issues/create` checks only that `issueType`, `category` and `description` are truthy, then trusts every field: no type checks, no length caps, no allowlist on `category` (which becomes a repo label), and `technicalInfo` fields are interpolated into the issue body unexamined. Zod is already a dependency and `shared/schema.ts` is the established pattern. Define a `bugReportSchema` with enums for `issueType`/`category` and length limits, and `safeParse` the body before use.
findings.issue_title: Validate the bug-report payload with a Zod schema
findings.issue_body: `server/routes/issues.ts:44-48` gates the endpoint on truthiness of three fields and otherwise trusts the payload: unbounded string lengths, no enum check on `category` (used to mint repo labels after a regex transform at `:63-67`), and `technicalInfo` values interpolated straight into the issue markdown. The repo already uses Zod for its data schemas. Add a `bugReportSchema` (enum `issueType`, allowlisted `category`, length-capped strings, optional screenshot as a validated data URL) and reject anything that fails `safeParse` with a 400.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes external input crossing into the system; `req.body` at `server/routes/issues.ts:32-41` is attacker-controlled JSON.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy anywhere, and Express fingerprint exposed
findings.body_md: Neither the app nor the proxy sets a `Content-Security-Policy` (verified against the live site: Caddy adds HSTS, `nosniff` and permissions-policy, but no CSP), and `x-powered-by: Express` is served, fingerprinting the stack. `TODO.md:36-39` believes a CSP is active ("CSP blocking eval... working as intended"), which is stale. Add `app.disable('x-powered-by')` and a CSP (self plus Google Fonts) either in Express or the Caddy vhost.
findings.issue_title: Add a Content-Security-Policy and disable the x-powered-by header
findings.issue_body: The live site serves no `Content-Security-Policy` header (checked 2026-08-18: Caddy adds HSTS, `x-content-type-options` and a permissions-policy, but no CSP) while `TODO.md:36-39` asserts one is active, and Express advertises itself via `x-powered-by`. Add `app.disable('x-powered-by')` in `server/index.ts` and set a CSP allowing self plus fonts.googleapis.com/fonts.gstatic.com, either in Express middleware or the Caddy vhost config, then correct TODO.md.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes layer boundaries needing named controls; the app serves HTML/JS to browsers through Express behind Caddy.

findings.title: The bug-report feature runs on a full-scope, non-expiring classic PAT
findings.body_md: `GITHUB_TOKEN_SETUP.md:9-15` instructs creating a classic personal access token with the full `repo` scope and "No expiration", stored in the server's `.env`. That credential can push to, delete from, and administer every repository the account owns; a compromise of this one container (whose only endpoint is public and unauthenticated) loses the whole GitHub account's repos. Replace it with a fine-grained PAT scoped to `rodlunt/choresandrewardsV2` with Issues read/write (plus Contents write only if screenshot commits stay), set an expiry, and update the doc.
findings.issue_title: Replace the full-scope classic PAT with a fine-grained, single-repo, expiring token
findings.issue_body: The bug-report feature authenticates with a classic PAT created per `GITHUB_TOKEN_SETUP.md:9-15`: full `repo` scope, no expiration, stored in the production `.env`. The endpoint that spends it (`server/routes/issues.ts`) is public and unauthenticated, so this token is the blast radius of any server compromise, and it currently covers every repository on the account. Mint a fine-grained PAT restricted to this repository with Issues: read/write (and Contents: write only if screenshot commits are kept), give it an expiry with a rotation reminder, replace the server value, revoke the old token, and update the setup doc.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes a server-held credential; the deployment stores `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the server's .env (server/routes/issues.ts:7) and the setup doc prescribes its shape.

findings.title: Unauthenticated endpoint lets anyone create issues and commit arbitrary files to the public repo
findings.body_md: `POST /api/issues/create` has no authentication, no rate limiting and no abuse controls. Any internet client can create unlimited labelled issues on the repo, and by sending a `screenshot` field starting with `data:image` can have arbitrary base64 content committed to the public `bug-report-screenshots` branch (`:114-157`) and served from raw.githubusercontent.com: the endpoint is a free anonymous file host under this GitHub account's name, with no check that the content is actually an image. Add per-IP rate limiting, verify the decoded content is a real image (magic bytes plus a size cap), and consider a lightweight shared secret or CAPTCHA on submission.
findings.issue_title: Rate-limit and content-validate /api/issues/create; it currently accepts anonymous writes into the repo
findings.issue_body: `server/routes/issues.ts:30` accepts POSTs from anyone with no rate limit or auth. Consequences: unlimited spam issues with attacker-chosen labels, and worse, the screenshot path (`:114-157`) commits whatever base64 follows a `data:image` prefix into the public `bug-report-screenshots` branch, publishing it via raw.githubusercontent.com under your account, with no verification that it is an image and no size cap beyond the JSON body limit. Add express-rate-limit (a few submissions per IP per hour), validate the decoded screenshot's magic bytes and cap its size, and gate submission behind at least a per-deployment shared token or CAPTCHA. Also decide whether screenshot hosting belongs in a public repo at all (see the privacy issue).
findings.precondition: The rule presumes requests carrying actions that need authorisation; `POST /api/issues/create` performs GitHub writes on behalf of any caller.

findings.title: Production container ships the full dev toolchain and runs TypeScript through tsx
findings.body_md: The production image deliberately keeps all devDependencies (`Dockerfile:25-26`: "Don't clean up dev dependencies - we need tsx"), executes TypeScript at runtime via `pnpm exec tsx server/index.ts` (`:40`), and copies the entire source tree in. The built server bundle that `pnpm run build` produces (`dist/index.js`) is created and then ignored. Result: vite, esbuild, tsx and the whole dev graph are present and loadable in production, enlarging the vulnerable surface the failing `pnpm audit` gate is measuring, and `server/vite.ts` statically imports the vite package even on the production path. Run the built `dist/index.js` (`pnpm run start`), prune dev deps in a multi-stage build, and fix the static vite import (Vite's own guidance is a dynamic import behind the dev check).
findings.issue_title: Production Docker image should run the built bundle, not tsx with devDependencies installed
findings.issue_body: `Dockerfile:25-40` installs all devDependencies, keeps them in the final image, and starts the app with `pnpm exec tsx server/index.ts`, while the `pnpm run build` output (`dist/index.js`) it just created goes unused. The production container therefore carries vite, esbuild, tsx and the full dev dependency graph (extra vulnerability surface for the same audit gate that blocks deploys), and `server/index.ts` statically imports `server/vite.ts`, which imports the `vite` package at module load even in production. Switch to a multi-stage build: build stage runs `pnpm run build`; runtime stage copies `dist/` and production node_modules only and runs `node dist/index.js`. Make the vite dev-server import dynamic (`await import("./vite")` behind the development check) so the bundle has no vite dependency.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes a production deployment whose configuration is attack surface; the Dockerfile builds the image `docker-compose.yml` runs in production.

findings.title: Docker base image pinned to a mutable tag, not a digest
findings.body_md: Dependencies are properly locked (`pnpm-lock.yaml` with `--frozen-lockfile`), but the base image `node:22-alpine` is a mutable tag re-resolved on every `docker-compose up --build`, so the production runtime can change under the same commit. Pin the base image by digest (`node:22-alpine@sha256:...`) and bump it deliberately.
findings.issue_title: Pin the Dockerfile base image by digest
findings.issue_body: `Dockerfile:2` uses `FROM node:22-alpine`, a mutable tag that is re-resolved on each rebuild, so two deploys of the same commit can run different runtimes and a registry-side compromise would flow straight into production. Application dependencies are already locked via `pnpm-lock.yaml`. Pin the base image with its digest (`FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:...`) and update the digest deliberately, mirroring the same reasoning as SHA-pinning GitHub Actions.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes build inputs that should be immutable; the production image builds `FROM node:22-alpine` on every deploy.

findings.title: Error responses forward internal error messages to the client
findings.body_md: `issues.ts:186-192` returns `error.message` from any failure (Octokit errors can carry request URLs, rate-limit state and repo details), and the global handler at `server/index.ts:42-48` echoes `err.message` for every unhandled error. Internals belong in the server log; the client gets a generic message and an correlation id if needed. Log the full error server-side and return a fixed "Failed to create issue" body.
findings.issue_title: Stop returning internal error.message values to API clients
findings.issue_body: `server/routes/issues.ts:186-192` responds with `error.message` on any failure, and the global Express handler (`server/index.ts:42-48`) does the same for all routes. GitHub client errors can include API URLs, rate-limit and repository detail that map the backend for an attacker probing the unauthenticated endpoint. Log the full error server-side; return only a fixed, generic message (optionally with a correlation id that matches the log line).
findings.precondition: The rule presumes errors crossing the trust boundary to callers; both the endpoint catch block and the global error handler respond to public clients.

findings.title: No security-relevant logging or alerting for the public endpoint
findings.body_md: The only logging is a truncated 80-character request line to stdout (`server/index.ts:20-34`). Validation failures, GitHub API failures and submission bursts are not distinguishable, and nothing alerts a human: abuse of the endpoint (mass issue creation, file-host abuse) would be discovered by browsing the repo. The homelab already runs ntfy and GlitchTip; wire endpoint errors into GlitchTip and add a simple burst alert (N submissions per hour) to ntfy.
findings.issue_title: Log and alert on bug-report endpoint failures and abuse
findings.issue_body: The server's only logging is a truncated request line (`server/index.ts:20-34`); rejected submissions, GitHub failures and abuse bursts are invisible unless someone happens to be watching the repo. Since the endpoint can be abused to create spam issues and commit files, add structured logs for rejected and failed submissions, report exceptions to the existing GlitchTip instance, and send an ntfy alert when submission volume exceeds a sane per-hour threshold.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes security-relevant events worth recording; the public issue-creation endpoint can be abused (spam, file uploads) and its failures matter.

self_assessment.limits: The express.json default body limit (100kb) likely also breaks large screenshot uploads functionally; not filed as a security finding. The Caddy vhost config for candr.lunt.au lives in another repo and was assessed only via live response headers.

coverage.note: All server code, input-handling client components, Dockerfile, compose file, workflows and token setup doc read; live site headers checked with curl. Stock shadcn/ui components skipped.

findings.title: Known dependency vulnerabilities unremediated for six weeks while the fixes sit in open Dependabot PRs
findings.body_md: The awareness and detection half of vulnerability management works here (Dependabot alerts, the CI `pnpm audit` gate), but remediation does not: 5 alerts are open, the audit gate has been red since 2026-07-05, and the fixes have been sitting in open Dependabot PRs #31 (nanoid) and #32 (postcss, the headline GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849) since 10-12 August, unmerged. The cycle stops at detection, so the vulnerable versions keep shipping (and keep blocking deploys). Merge the Dependabot PRs, re-run `pnpm audit` for the remainder, and adopt a habit of acting on alerts within days, since this repo's gate makes ignoring them expensive.
findings.issue_title: Merge the open Dependabot PRs and clear the six-week-old vulnerability backlog
findings.issue_body: GitHub shows 5 open Dependabot alerts, and the `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` CI gate has failed on every run since 2026-07-05. The fixes for the two headline packages already exist as open Dependabot PRs: #31 (nanoid 5.1.6 to 5.1.16, open since 2026-08-10) and #32 (postcss 8.5.16 to 8.5.23, open since 2026-08-12, addressing GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849). Merge both, run `pnpm audit` locally to identify what remains (transitive paths may need `pnpm.overrides` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`), and clear the rest. Detection is wired up and working; the gap is that nothing acts on it.

findings.title: The only copy of family data lives in one browser profile with an unbounded loss window
findings.body_md: All user data is client-side IndexedDB and nothing bounds the loss window: the app never calls `navigator.storage.persist()` (verified by grep), so browsers may evict the database under storage pressure, and clearing site data, a lost device or the documented "users must delete IndexedDB to upgrade" path (`db.ts:59-60`) erases everything. The only mitigation is a manual export button nobody is prompted to use. Request persistent storage on startup, and prompt for (or automate) periodic export so the recovery point is days rather than forever.
findings.issue_title: Guard against silent total data loss: request persistent storage and prompt for backups
findings.issue_body: Every child, balance and payout lives only in the visitor's browser IndexedDB (`client/src/lib/db.ts`); the server stores nothing. The app never calls `navigator.storage.persist()`, so the browser is free to evict the database under storage pressure, and site-data clearing or device loss wipes the family's history with no recovery. The export feature exists but is manual and unprompted. Call `navigator.storage.persist()` during startup, surface whether persistence was granted, and add a periodic reminder (or automatic download) of the JSON export so the worst-case loss window is bounded.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes data whose acceptable loss window should be defined; the app's children, balances and payout history exist solely in the user's browser IndexedDB (client/src/lib/db.ts), with no server copy.

findings.title: Checked-in recovery tooling is stale and destructive: rollback script force-pushes main to an October 2025 commit
findings.body_md: `rollback-to-working.sh` hard-resets to the hardcoded commit `f68a540` (October 2025) and runs `git push origin main --force`: executed today it would obliterate ten months of history on main. `.github/DEPLOYMENT.md`'s rollback procedure targets the old Windows homeserver (`E:/Prod`, port 2223, npm commands) that no longer hosts the app, which now lives on a tailnet-only Linux server (issue #29). In an incident, both artefacts read as authoritative and both are wrong. Delete the two rollback scripts, and rewrite DEPLOYMENT.md's recovery section for the current host (git checkout of a known-good tag plus `docker compose up -d --build`).
findings.issue_title: Delete the stale force-push rollback scripts and fix the recovery docs for the current host
findings.issue_body: `rollback-to-working.sh:18-19` does `git reset --hard f68a540 && git push origin main --force`, pinned to a commit from October 2025; running it now would force main back ten months. `rollback.ps1` is its Windows twin, and `.github/DEPLOYMENT.md`'s rollback section documents SSH to the retired Windows homeserver (`E:/Prod/ChoresandRewards`, port 2223) with npm commands, none of which matches the current tailnet-only Linux host. These are the documents someone would follow mid-incident. Delete both scripts, and replace the DEPLOYMENT.md recovery section with the real procedure for the current server: check out a known-good commit or tag and `docker compose up -d --build`, with the deploy path named.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes recovery procedures meant to be followed under pressure; the repo ships `rollback-to-working.sh`, `rollback.ps1` and a rollback section in `.github/DEPLOYMENT.md` as exactly that.

findings.title: Endpoint collapses outcomes to 200/400/500
findings.body_md: Successful creation returns 200 with a body instead of 201, and a missing `GITHUB_TOKEN` (a service-configuration state) returns the same 500 shape as an unexpected fault. findings.title: No recorded decision on who may use the API to publish under the owner's GitHub account
findings.body_md: The endpoint works exactly as designed while granting any anonymous caller the ability to publish content (issues, labels, screenshot files) that appears under the repository owner's account. The mechanical fixes (rate limiting, content validation) are filed from the security review; this finding asks for the governance half: decide and record who may submit, at what volume, and what happens to submissions (moderation, retention, takedown).
findings.issue_title: Decide and record the access policy for bug-report submissions

findings.title: Deploy takes the site down before building, extending every deploy's outage to the length of the image build
findings.body_md: The deploy sequence is `docker-compose down` then `docker-compose up -d --build`: the container stops first and the (multi-minute pnpm install and vite build) image build happens while the site is dead. Removing the `down` step (or running `docker-compose build` first, then `up -d`) shrinks the outage to a container restart. In-place deployment is a fine choice at this scale; the ordering is just paying for downtime it does not need to.
findings.issue_title: Build the image before stopping the container in the deploy script
findings.issue_body: Both deploy workflows run `docker-compose down` followed by `docker-compose up -d --build`, so the production site is down for the entire image build (pnpm install plus vite build, minutes) on every deploy. Compose can build while the old container serves: replace the pair with `docker-compose build && docker-compose up -d` (or simply `docker-compose up -d --build`, which recreates after building), cutting each deploy's outage to a restart.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes a rollout strategy being chosen for a production deploy; the deploy script runs on every push to main.

findings.title: Required configuration is checked lazily at request time instead of failing fast at startup
findings.body_md: `GITHUB_TOKEN` is only checked when a user submits a report: a deployment missing the variable starts cleanly, reports healthy (the healthcheck only curls `/`), and fails the first user with a 500. Validate required configuration at startup and log loudly (or refuse to start) when it is absent, so a misconfigured deploy is caught at deploy time, not by a user.
findings.issue_title: Validate GITHUB_TOKEN at startup instead of on first submission
findings.issue_body: `server/routes/issues.ts:50-55` discovers a missing `GITHUB_TOKEN` only when someone submits a bug report; the container starts, passes its healthcheck (which only curls `/`), and the misconfiguration surfaces as a user-facing 500 whenever the first report arrives. Check required environment variables at startup in `server/index.ts` and either exit non-zero or log an unmissable warning, so a bad deploy fails at deploy time.
findings.precondition: The rule presumes environment-supplied configuration; GITHUB_TOKEN is read from the environment at server/routes/issues.ts:7.

self_assessment.limits: The build-during-downtime claim assumes no image cache makes the rebuild near-instant on the host; even fully cached, the down-first ordering still serialises outage with build.

findings.title: Import destroys all data with no confirmation, and an accidental chore completion cannot be undone
findings.body_md: Two irreversible actions lack the protection the reversible-checked-confirmed rule requires. Import (`SettingsPage.tsx:107-136`) clears children, chores and payouts and replaces them the moment a file is chosen: no confirmation naming what will be destroyed, no undo, no automatic pre-import export. Completing a chore (`ChildChoresPage.tsx:257-264`) adds to a child's balance with a single tap on a child-operated screen, and the app offers no way to reverse it: no undo, and no UI anywhere to decrement a total, so a double-tap or wrong-row tap permanently inflates the balance. Add a confirmation to import that names the replaced data (and auto-export first), and add an undo (toast with Undo, or a completion ledger with delete) for completions.
findings.issue_title: Add confirmation/auto-backup to import and an undo for chore completions
findings.issue_body: Two destructive interactions have no way back. (1) Import backup (`client/src/pages/SettingsPage.tsx:107-136`): selecting a file immediately clears all children, chores and payouts and writes the file's contents, with no confirmation stating that current data will be replaced, no undo and no automatic backup of what is about to be destroyed. Confirm with the scope named ("Replace 2 children, 24 chores and 15 payouts?") and export the current data automatically before importing. (2) Chore completion (`client/src/pages/ChildChoresPage.tsx:257-264`): one tap permanently adds the chore's value to a balance, the screen is designed for children, and no mechanism exists anywhere to reverse or adjust it. Show an Undo action in the completion toast, or record completions and allow deleting one.

findings.title: Known accessibility failures have sat in the backlog for ten months as deferred polish
